transcript.text: Thank you all for being here. As we all know, we're facing a trade secrets misappropriation lawsuit from a former employee, and the complaint is seeking broad inspection of our devices and systems. We have an initial case-management conference coming up next month, and no discovery has been exchanged yet. Our priorities are clear: protect the company's confidential information and keep defense costs under control. Before I approve the initial defense plan, I need each of you to identify any facts that should shape our approach. Discovery counsel, let's start with you — what do we need to know? And insurance-coverage counsel, I want to hear from you as well. What facts should I be considering before signing off on this plan?

The review confirmed that exactly three identified trade-secret files were copied to the device. Importantly, the review found no customer data on the device and no evidence of any additional copying beyond those three files. My report is currently awaiting final partner review and has not yet been added to the case plan. This finding should significantly shape our defense strategy — it narrows the scope of exposure considerably and gives us leverage to push back against the broad inspection demands in the complaint.

transcript.text: Elena, I need to flag an important coverage issue before we proceed. I've reviewed the applicable policy endorsement, and the trade-secret defense is covered subject to a $75,000 self-insured retention, insurer-approved panel counsel, and a requirement that we obtain written insurer consent before engaging any forensic vendor. The endorsement is currently stored in the risk department's file and has not been attached to this matter. This directly affects our defense plan: we need to ensure we're using insurer-approved counsel to preserve coverage, and critically, any forensic vendor engagement must receive written insurer consent first. Samir's forensic review may already implicate this consent requirement, so we need to address that promptly.

Morgan, your coverage analysis is critical and raises an immediate concern. Samir's forensic review may have been conducted without the written insurer consent required by the endorsement. We need to determine right now whether that consent was obtained, and if not, we need to cure that issue immediately to preserve coverage. Before I approve the defense plan, here's what I need from each of you: Samir, please get your report through partner review and added to the case plan, and confirm whether the forensic vendor engagement went through any approval process. Morgan, please pull the endorsement from risk and attach it to this matter, and initiate the insurer consent process for the forensic vendor retroactively if needed. My preliminary thinking is this: we should seek a narrow protective order limiting discovery to the three identified files and the specific device, we should not need to produce customer data given Samir's findings, and we must use insurer-approved panel counsel to preserve coverage. But I will not sign off until the coverage consent issue is addressed and the forensic report is finalized. Are there any other facts I should know before we proceed?

That's something we need to verify urgently, and I will work with Morgan to initiate the retroactive consent process if it wasn't secured. I should also note that the scope of my forensic review was limited to the former employee's company laptop — I have not examined any personal devices, cloud accounts, or external storage that the former employee may have used. The three-file finding gives us strong leverage for a narrow protective order, but we should be prepared for plaintiff's counsel to argue that the laptop review doesn't conclusively establish the full scope of any alleged misappropriation. I don't have any additional private facts to disclose at this time, but I want to make sure we're all aware of that scope limitation as we shape the defense plan.
